summary: Arkansas sets no special smoke or CO alarm step at sale, but the statewide fire code already requires an approved listed smoke alarm in every home, new or existing, including one- and two-family houses.
alarmType: Listed single- and multiple-station smoke alarms complying with UL 217, installed per NFPA 72 and fire code sections 907.2.11.1 to 907.2.11.7. In new construction the required alarms must draw primary power from the building wiring where it is served from a commercial source, with battery backup, on permanent wiring with no disconnect other than overcurrent protection, and must chirp when the battery is low. Where more than one alarm is required they must be interconnected so one alarm sets off all of them; listed wireless alarms that all sound together satisfy this instead of physical interconnection. The existing-dwelling rule (R314.2.3 of the residential volume) requires only 'an approved listed smoke alarm' and does not impose the hardwiring or sealed-battery specifications.
coAlarms: Not tied to sale. Under fire code section 915, CO detection must be installed in new buildings in R occupancies (dwellings) and certain institutional and school occupancies wherever a dwelling unit contains a fuel-burning appliance or fuel-burning fireplace, is served by a fuel-burning forced-air furnace, or sits in a building containing such equipment with communicating openings. In dwelling units the detection goes outside each separate sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, and inside a bedroom if a fuel-burning appliance is in the bedroom or its attached bathroom. Existing buildings are handled under section 1103.9, which was not read.
citation: Arkansas Fire Prevention Code (2021 edition), Vol. I section 907.2.11 and Vol. III section R314.2.3 (smoke alarms in every new and existing dwelling, including one- and two-family dwellings); section 915 (CO detection). Promulgated by the Director of the Division of Arkansas State Police under A.C.A. 12-13-105 (Section 6 of Act 254 of 1955).
lastAmended: 2021 edition of the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code, superseding the 2012 edition. Confirmed as the currently applicable state fire and building code (which includes the Residential Code, based on the 2021 I-codes with Arkansas amendments) by the state's 'Current Applicable State Codes in Arkansas' list at https://sas.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/CurrentCodes072023.pdf
notVerified: The Arkansas Code (statutes) could not be searched at all. The Arkansas General Assembly does not publish the Arkansas Code on its own site; arkleg.state.ar.us links out to the commercial official publisher (LexisNexis), which requires cookies and JavaScript and is not a .gov source, so it was not used. A statutory smoke- or CO-alarm requirement tied to sale could therefore exist in the Arkansas Code without being found here. Treat 'no requirement at sale' as unconfirmed on the statutory side.

The source document read is the Arkansas State Police rule-change filing for the 2021 Arkansas Fire Prevention Code, which shows the Arkansas amendments to the model code with strikethroughs and underlining. Its signature block shows the effective date as 'TBD' because it is the filing copy. The unamended model-code text (IFC/IBC/IRC 2021), including residential section R315 on CO alarms and fire code section 1103.9 on CO detection in existing buildings, is incorporated by reference and was not read.
No certification, inspection or affidavit requirement at sale was found, but this follows from finding no sale provision at all rather than from reading a provision that says none is needed.

How the existing-dwelling smoke alarm rule is actually enforced on owner-occupied houses. The code order itself urges Arkansas cities and counties to adopt the fire code as a local ordinance, which suggests enforcement depends partly on local adoption; this was not verified.
A 2019 bill (HB 1410) adding landlord habitability duties to Arkansas Code Title 18, Chapter 17 was located but its final disposition and any smoke-alarm content were not traced.
